claim: The earlier brief cites PMC4539330 as Norman 2014 (30% slower, n 96 and 108). That page is a different study: 47 residents, quick first pass then optional self-directed reflection. Only 8% of diagnoses were revised and the score moved from 1.20 to 1.22.
quote: Participants did engage in self-directed reflection for incorrect diagnoses.
authors: not shown in fetch
title: Residents' self-directed reflection and revised diagnoses (title not shown in fetch)
transfer: Fix the citation. Lesson: when the model may revise its own answer, it rarely does and the gain is tiny, so a revision step needs a trigger, not a schedule.

claim: Norman et al 2014: telling residents to work slowly and carefully did not raise accuracy over telling them to work fast, across two cohorts from three Canadian schools. The careful group took longer. Accuracy correlated inversely with time spent.
authors: Norman GR, Sherbino J, Dore K, et al.
title: The etiology of diagnostic errors: a controlled trial of system 1 versus system 2 reasoning
n: two cohorts of second-year residents (exact n not confirmed)
transfer: Do not add a slow-down or be-careful instruction as a default step. Compare against a plain call at equal tokens.

claim: The brief's numbers n of 96 and 108 and 30% longer for Norman 2014 were not confirmed in this round. The fetched abstract summary gives only: accuracy essentially the same under both instructions, reflective group slower.
authors: Norman GR et al.
title: The etiology of diagnostic errors (Europe PMC record)
transfer: none (audit note: treat the 30% and sample sizes as unverified)

claim: Guided reflection with 6 or 2 generated alternative diagnoses did not improve strict accuracy over first impressions in 186 medical students. Short 0.42, long 0.41, control 0.47. Lenient scoring showed 0.70 and 0.72 vs 0.47.
quote: did not elicit more accurate final diagnoses than diagnosis based on first impressions only
authors: Lambe KA et al.
title: Guided reflection and diagnostic accuracy (Frontiers in Psychology)
transfer: Scoring rule decides whether reflection looks good. Grade the agent strictly. Do not trust a lenient grader to approve a doubt step.

claim: In the same Lambe 2018 study, reflection changed answers in both directions. Short condition had 16 corrections and 26 backfires. Long condition had 14 corrections and 14 backfires. No significant difference.
authors: Lambe KA et al.
title: Guided reflection and diagnostic accuracy (Frontiers in Psychology)
transfer: Log corrections vs backfires for every revise step. Keep a revise step only if corrections beat backfires by a margin on held-out items.

claim: Kämmer 2021: a differential checklist raised accuracy only when it held the correct diagnosis (0.75 vs 0.49 control). Without it, 0.43. A prompt to list and rank your own differentials gave 0.53, not significant. Neither changed information gathering or self-monitoring.
quote: the correct diagnosis needs to be on the checklist
authors: Kämmer JE, Schauber SK, Hautz SC, Stroben F, Hautz WE
title: Differential diagnosis checklists reduce diagnostic error differentially: A randomised experiment
transfer: Confirms the brief. Own-list prompting did nothing. An outside source of candidates is the only part that helped.

claim: Sibbald 2019: debiasing and knowledge-retrieval checklists were each randomized against no checklist on 20 ECGs, half bias-inducing. Neither beat control overall. They may help novices. The brief's recalled claim that retrieval checklists beat debiasing ones is not supported by the abstract.
authors: Sibbald M, Sherbino J, Ilgen JS, Zwaan L, Blissett S, Monteiro S, Norman G
title: Debiasing versus knowledge retrieval checklists to reduce diagnostic error in ECG interpretation
n: residents and cardiology fellows (n not captured)
transfer: Checklist-style steps are a null on average. Any checklist step must prove itself on novice-like (weak) cases only, if at all.

claim: A debiasing workshop for family medicine residents improved 1 of 4 outcomes. Diagnostic concordance 74% vs 78% (p=0.64), bias recognition 51% vs 57% (p=0.46), unrecognized bias 12% vs 9% (p=0.55). Only writing a mitigation plan improved (84% to 100%).
quote: improvement in one of four studied outcomes
authors: Smith BW, Slack MB
title: The effect of cognitive debiasing training among family medicine residents
transfer: Knowing about bias changes what people say about bias, not what they diagnose. A prompt that names biases is likely to change wording, not answers.

claim: Systematic review of dual-process interventions: 28 studies in five categories. Guided reflection was the most consistent across five studies, cognitive forcing improved accuracy and confidence, but measures varied widely and most subjects were early-career. Authors call results promising, not firm.
authors: Lambe KA et al.
title: Dual-process cognitive interventions to enhance diagnostic reasoning: a systematic review
transfer: The positive review sits beside the null trials above. Weight single large controlled trials over the review's vote count.

claim: A later systematic review of debiasing and educational interventions in diagnosis found mixed results across tools, bias education and debiasing-strategy education. 17 of 2,232 records included. No included study measured clinical-setting decisions or long-term follow-up.
authors: Tung A, Melchiorre M
title: Debiasing and Educational Interventions in Medical Diagnosis: A Systematic Review
transfer: Debias-by-instruction has no strong evidence base even in humans. Do not hard-code it.

claim: Graber 2005: in 100 internal-medicine error cases, premature closure was the most common cognitive cause, and knowledge gaps were rarely the problem. 33 cases ended in death. This is a case review, so it shows where errors cluster, not that a fix works.
quote: Diagnostic error is commonly multifactorial in origin, typically involving both system-related and cognitive factors.
authors: Graber ML, Franklin N, Gordon R
title: Diagnostic error in internal medicine
transfer: Error taxonomy only. It is selected from known errors, so base rates of closure in correct cases are unknown. Do not infer that more doubt helps.

claim: Norman 2009 argues dual-process systems perform about equally well and that prompting use of both can consistently reduce error. This sits against the later null trials and shows the recommended method was argued before it was tested.
authors: Norman G
title: Dual processing and diagnostic errors
transfer: none

claim: GPT-4 on 70 NEJM cases put the final diagnosis in its differential 64% of the time (45/70) but ranked it first only 39% (27/70). Mean rank when present was 2.5. Confirms the brief's memory number and adds the top-1 gap.
quote: The AI model's top diagnosis agreed with the final diagnosis in 39% (27/70) of cases.
authors: Kanjee Z, Crowe B, Rodman A
title: Accuracy of a Generative Artificial Intelligence Model in a Complex Diagnostic Challenge
transfer: Large gap between candidate recall and top-1 selection. A selection step has headroom, but only if it can rank better than the model's own order.

claim: Goh 2024 RCT: GPT-4 plus conventional resources scored 76% vs 74% for resources alone (adjusted difference 2 points, 95% CI -4 to 8, P=.60). The LLM alone scored 92%, 16 points above the conventional group.
quote: The LLM alone demonstrated higher performance than both physician groups.
authors: Goh E et al.
title: Large language model influence on diagnostic reasoning: a randomized clinical trial
transfer: A model's good answer is lost when a weaker reader decides. Let the program, not a second weaker judge step, make the final pick. Beware our own critic call acting as that weaker reader.

claim: UK replication of the Goh design: physicians with LLM access scored 74.3% vs 65.7% with conventional resources (p=0.001), better than the US null, but 21.3 points below the LLM alone. Only 30% of questions were put to the LLM. The preprint version had different numbers.
authors: Healy J, Kossoff J, Lee M, Hasford C
title: Human-AI collaboration in clinical reasoning: a UK replication and interaction analysis
transfer: The gap between assisted and alone is the human integration step. In an agent, remove the integration step: use the model's answer unless a hard check fails.

claim: In a crossover study of 30 ophthalmology cases with Claude-3.5-Sonnet, mean accuracy rose from 0.45 to 0.60, but 20% of participants got worse. The LLM alone scored 0.70. In failures, 58.6% followed an incorrect LLM insight that the human accepted.
authors: Ong KT, Seo J, Kim H, et al.
title: Success and failure of human-AI collaboration in clinical reasoning: An experimental study on challenging real-world cases
venue: Int J Med Inform 211:106342 (an erratum exists, vol. 212)
transfer: A wrong confident first suggestion is accepted by the next reader. Same risk for a second agent call that sees the first answer. Keep checks blind to it.

claim: BiasMedQA: 1,273 USMLE questions with seven injected biases, six models. GPT-4 dropped about 5%, Llama 2 70B-chat about 20%, with false-consensus bias the worst (average -24.9%). Bias education gave +3.5 to +6.5 points for most models but -0.1 for PMC Llama 13B. Mitigations did not restore accuracy. The paper's tables are inconsistent in places.
quote: improved but did not fully restore accuracy
authors: Schmidgall S et al.
title: Evaluation and mitigation of cognitive biases in medical language models
transfer: Strip leading framing from inputs and ask the question neutrally. Prompting 'beware bias' gives only partial recovery, so remove the bias in the program instead.

claim: Hager et al: on 2,400 real MIMIC-IV abdominal cases, frontier LLMs diagnosed significantly worse than physicians, did not follow guidelines, could not interpret labs, and were sensitive to the quantity and order of information.
authors: Hager P et al.
title: Evaluation and mitigation of the limitations of large language models in clinical decision-making
transfer: Exam-style wins do not carry to open information gathering. Shuffle the order of evidence across samples to expose order sensitivity before trusting an answer.

claim: MAI-DxO with o3 reports 80% (85.5% at max-accuracy setting) vs 20% for generalist physicians on 304 NEJM cases, and 20% lower cost than physicians. Caveats in the abstract: virtual costs, hard cases, simulated gatekeeper. No ablation separating panel structure from extra compute was in the abstract.
quote: achieves 80% diagnostic accuracy--four times higher than the 20% average of generalist physicians.
authors: Microsoft AI (Nori H et al.; author list not checked)
title: Sequential Diagnosis with Language Models
transfer: Treat as an unreplicated vendor result. If copied, run the equal-token ablation ourselves.

claim: Test-time scaling study in medical LLMs: longer reasoning is not always better. For non-reasoning LLMs accuracy saturated quickly. Models abandoned correct reasoning when given misleading expert hints.
quote: Longer reasoning is not universally beneficial.
authors: Oh G, Kim S, Park S, Kim BH
title: Test-time scaling in medical LLMs and VLMs
transfer: Cap thinking budget on single-answer items. Never feed a model an unverified 'expert hint' in a check step.

claim: A randomized simulation with 13 physicians and 260 consultations: an AI diagnostic copilot raised top-3 accuracy (74.6% vs 62.3%) but not top-1 (57% vs 47.8%, p=.08). Consultation time rose 10.7%. Concordance with wrong AI advice was 55.8% vs 38.8%, not significant.
authors: Cusacovich I, Pinilla M, Garcia Castro R
title: Real-Time Artificial Intelligence Diagnostic Copilot in Simulated Primary Care Consultations: Randomized Simulation Study
transfer: Aids widen the candidate list (top-3) more than they fix the final pick (top-1). Same shape as our M1.

claim: Prompting can hurt: in a 300-case hypertension study, zero-shot prompting gave 62.7% with DeepSeek-V3 vs 91.3% for the best setup, and the worst LLM setups pushed physicians' inappropriate regimen rate from 26.6% to 35.2%.
quote: increasing inappropriate regimen rates from 26.6% to 35.2%
authors: Li Z, Liu H, Tan W, et al.
title: Multitype prompt engineering for hypertension treatment decisions
transfer: Self-consistency style structure helped here, but simulated cases and a treatment task. Do not extend to diagnosis without our own test.

claim: In a TCM chain-of-thought plus retrieval ablation, removing any reasoning module dropped performance below the zero-shot baseline, though the full pipeline helped. Partial schemas can be worse than none.
quote: removing any reasoning module caused performance collapse below the zero-shot baseline
authors: Fan B, Fang Y, Wang Z, Ma F
title: TCM-CoT-RAG
transfer: Ablate each schema step on its own. A half-built schema may lose to plain, as our 0% scaffold did.

claim: Medprompt (dynamic few-shot, self-generated CoT, choice-shuffle ensemble) reports state of the art on all nine MultiMedQA datasets with GPT-4. This is an exam-style benchmark, and the abstract does not say which part caused the gain.
quote: With Medprompt, GPT-4 achieves state-of-the-art results on all nine of the benchmark datasets in the MultiMedQA suite.
authors: Nori H et al.
title: Can Generalist Foundation Models Outcompete Special-Purpose Tuning?
transfer: Choice-shuffle ensembling is the one cheap anti-anchoring part. Test it alone on our single-answer sets.
